studentLoanRepayment.title: Student Loan Repayment Calculator
studentLoanRepayment.subtitle: Enter your salary to see the mandatory repayment (monthly payroll deduction) and payoff date of a Korean income-contingent student loan, compared with the monthly payment and total interest of a standard loan, as of 2026.

input.title: Loan and income

kindHint.icl: Once your income exceeds the repayment threshold, a share of the excess is deducted from your pay.
kindHint.gen: After the grace period you pay the same amount every month (level payment) for a fixed term.

input.balanceHint: Remaining principal, in units of 10,000 KRW. Check it on the Korea Student Aid Foundation website or app.

rateHint.icl: 1.7% for both 2026 semesters (frozen). Income-contingent loans use a variable rate set each semester.
rateHint.gen: 1.7% for both 2026 semesters (frozen). Standard loans keep the rate fixed at the time of borrowing.

input.salaryHint: Including non-taxable pay, in units of 10,000 KRW. Later years grow by the rate below.
input.nontaxHint: Meal allowance (up to 200,000 KRW a month) etc. Total pay = salary − non-taxable pay

startHint.icl: The year your income starts. The calculation starts from the January balance, and that year's income is the first to be assessed.
startHint.gen: The remaining grace period and repayment term start in January of this year.

input.degreeHint: Repayment rate: 20% for undergraduate loans, 25% for graduate loans
input.free: I qualify for the interest exemption
input.freeHint: Basic livelihood recipients, near-poverty households, families with 3+ children, support bracket 6 or below, bracket 8 or below at non-capital-area universities, etc. Interest is skipped until mandatory repayment starts.
input.genHint: Up to 20 years (10-year grace + 10-year repayment). Only interest is paid during the grace period.
input.growthHint: An assumption. Your salary is assumed to grow by this rate every year.
input.thrGrowthHint: An assumption. Official thresholds for 2023–2026 rose 5.5–6.5% a year, following the standard median income.

compare.title: Both types under the same conditions
compare.caption: Income-contingent vs standard repayment
compare.iclNever: Under these assumptions the income-contingent loan is not repaid within {n} years. When income is close to the threshold, the mandatory repayment is similar to the interest and the balance barely falls.
compare.same: Under these conditions both types cost about the same in interest.
compare.genLess: Under these conditions the standard loan costs {v} less in interest. In exchange you must pay {pay} every month regardless of income.
compare.iclLess: Under these conditions the income-contingent loan costs {v} less in interest. As your income rises, deductions rise too and the loan ends sooner.
points: Income-contingent: no mandatory repayment in years your income is at or below the threshold, and you can apply for a deferral after job loss, business closure or parental leave. With a low income, though, repayment takes longer and interest grows.
Standard: a fixed rate and a fixed end date. You must pay the set amount every month even if your income stops.
Both can be prepaid at any time without a fee.
Results change a lot with your salary, growth and rate assumptions. Rather than declaring a winner, weigh your income outlook against what you can afford each month.

howTo.title: How to use
items: Pick a repayment type and enter the balance, rate and salary; results update instantly.

For the income-contingent loan, set the first year to the year your income starts. The mandatory repayment assessed on that year's income is deducted from your pay for 12 months from the following July.
Non-taxable pay such as meal allowances is excluded from total pay, so enter it as monthly non-taxable pay.
For the standard loan, choose the remaining grace period and repayment term to see the monthly payment and total interest. The comparison table below puts both types side by side.
Your inputs are stored in the URL, so you can share the link as is.

method.title: How it is calculated
items: Mandatory repayment = (annual income amount − repayment threshold) × repayment rate. The rate is 20% for undergraduate loans and 25% for graduate loans (Enforcement Decree Art. 10(1)).
With only employment income, income amount = total pay − earned income deduction. Total pay is your salary minus non-taxable pay.
The 2026 threshold is 30.37 million KRW in total pay, or 20,564,500 KRW as an income amount. In 2025 it was 28.51 million KRW in total pay (18.98 million KRW income amount).
If the calculated amount is below 360,000 KRW a year, the minimum of 360,000 KRW applies (Decree Art. 10(2)). If the remaining balance is smaller, you pay only the balance.
The National Tax Service sends the notice around April of the following year, and your employer deducts 1/12 of it from each paycheck from July through the next June (Decree Art. 21(3)).
Interest on income-contingent loans is simple interest on the balance. Here payments are assumed to clear accrued interest first, calculated monthly (the foundation calculates daily).
The standard loan charges interest only during the grace period, then level payments of principal and interest.

The 2027 threshold has not been announced. Because the 2023–2026 increases matched the 4-person standard median income increases, the 2027 increase of 6.7% is applied for an estimate of 32.40 million KRW.

tips.title: Good to know
items: Voluntary payments to the foundation in a year are subtracted from the mandatory repayment on that year's income. Paying less than the mandatory amount keeps the total the same but moves it earlier, trimming interest a little.
Before payroll deductions start, you can pay the mandatory amount in full or in two halves (Act Art. 24(7)); your employer may then not be notified.

Students from basic livelihood or near-poverty households, families with 3+ children, support bracket 6 or below (from July 1, 2026) or bracket 8 or below at non-capital-area universities (from November 20, 2026) are exempt from interest until graduation and the start of mandatory repayment.
If job loss, business closure or parental leave makes repayment hard, you can apply for a deferral, and interest during the deferral is waived.
At 65 or older, with no income other than the national pension and other conditions met, the remaining obligation can be waived (Act Art. 16(2)).
The income-contingent rate is variable and set every semester. If it changes, so does this calculation.

items.a: If your annual income amount exceeds the repayment threshold, you must repay 20% of the excess (25% for graduate loans); that is the mandatory repayment. If the calculated amount is below 360,000 KRW, it is 360,000 KRW. If your income amount is at or below the threshold, it is zero and repayment is postponed, but interest keeps accruing unless you are exempt.

items.q: How does it relate to the year-end tax settlement?
items.a: The mandatory repayment is assessed on the previous year's employment income as finalized in the year-end settlement (Decree Art. 19). It is notified separately from any tax refund or extra tax, and your employer deducts it over 12 months from July. Student loan principal and interest you repay yourself qualify for the education tax credit (15%, no limit) as your own education expenses.

items.q: What about freelancers and business owners?
items.a: The mandatory repayment is set within three months after the comprehensive income tax filing deadline, and you pay it yourself within 30 days of the notice (Act Art. 23). The income amount is business revenue minus necessary expenses. Business income subject to year-end settlement (insurance agents, etc.) can be deducted at source like a salary. This calculator assumes employment income only.

To emigrate you must report it at least three months before leaving and repay the full principal and interest at least one month before. If you cannot, you may be asked for installment repayment and collateral (Act Art. 20). For study abroad of six months or more, report your study and repayment plans at least 40 days before leaving (Act Art. 21).

items.q: What happens if I pay late?
items.a: Missing the payment deadline adds a 2% late charge on the unpaid amount, plus 0.5% each further month, up to 5% in total (Act Art. 30, Decree Art. 33). If you still do not pay after a demand notice, it can be collected by seizure in the same way as delinquent national taxes (Act Art. 32).

items.q: What if I lose my job or take parental leave?
items.a: If job loss or retirement, business closure, parental leave or a disaster makes things hard, you can apply to the tax office for a deferral after receiving the notice. The deferral lasts until the end of the year in which two years have passed since the application, and interest during that time is waived. While enrolled at a university or graduate school, you can apply for a four-year deferral regardless of hardship (Act Art. 18(7), Decree Art. 10-2).

Basic livelihood recipients and near-poverty households, children of families with 3+ children, youths leaving care, students in support bracket 6 (130% of the standard median income) or below, and students at non-capital-area universities in bracket 8 (200%) or below are exempt from interest until they graduate and their income exceeds the threshold (Act Art. 16-2(2)). Bracket 6 applies to interest from July 1, 2026 and the non-capital-area bracket 8 to interest from November 20, 2026. Interest during military service is also waived.
